r6-account.rival: There is no RL-specific policy of finishing before the cap: at T 1.0 the cued base's cap hits are simply the hard, long end of the one difficulty axis, and any arm that is stronger on that axis fixes them at the rate its overall strength predicts for problems of the same base difficulty. That arm can be RL, the top-8 edit, or the reward-free Think-SFT. So the budget share sits above the null because the other side is stronger on hard problems, not because RL learned to stop in time; the loop part is the same axis seen through a truncating sampler.

rows.experiment: MATH-500, claimed cell: RL's solve rate on the cued base's T1 cap-hit problems minus the solve rate expected for problems of the same base difficulty, using RL's rate on T1 finished-wrong problems with the same 4-sample base count
rows.theory_should_say: The theory says RL adds a policy of finishing long problems the base runs past the cap on, so at matched base difficulty RL should rescue cap hits well above its rate on finished-wrong problems, about +0.2. Under the single axis, the cap hits are just the low-k4 problems and the difference is near 0.

rows.experiment: hard328: RL plain's solve rate on the cued base's cap-hit problems minus the solve rate expected for problems of the same base difficulty, using RL's rate on the base's finished-wrong problems with the same count of right answers in three base-like cued resamples
rows.theory_should_say: The theory's budget part credits Math-RL, trained with truncated rollouts as negatives, with finishing the long problems the base runs out on, so at matched base difficulty RL should rescue base cap hits more often than finished-wrong problems, a positive difference of about +0.1. Under the single axis these cap hits are the longest problems, hard for RL too (it uses 13,155 tokens there and hits the cap itself on 11), so the matched difference is slightly negative.

rows.experiment: Budget share of the gap when the other side is the reward-free Think-SFT model with the cue: among problems Think-SFT cue gets right and the cued base's T1 gets wrong, the fraction where T1 is a cap hit
rows.theory_should_say: In the theory the budget part above the null is RL's learned finishing policy. Think-SFT has no reward and no truncation negatives, and it hits the cap itself about as often as the cued base (25 vs 27), so its budget share should sit at the null, about 0.11-0.15. Under the single axis Think-SFT is nearly as strong as RL, and stronger on long problems, so it fixes the base's cap hits about as RL does, giving a share near 0.20.

rows.experiment: MATH-500, T 1.0: on the cued base's T1 cap-hit problems, Think-SFT cue's right count minus Math-RL's (T2) right count
rows.theory_should_say: The theory credits the budget part to Math-RL's training on truncated rollouts as negatives. Think-SFT has no such training, and its own misses are cap hits on the longest problems, so it should fix the T1 cap hits at about the null rate plus a little: about 8 of 27 against RL's 16, a difference near -8 (the advocate's 0.13 share of a gap of about 60). This rival puts Think-SFT near RL, at about -1.

rows.experiment: MATH-500, T 1.0: Think-SFT cue's solve rate on the cued base's T1 cap-hit problems minus its solve rate on T1 finished-wrong problems of the same 4-sample base count (the matched excess, now for the reward-free arm)
rows.theory_should_say: With no RL finishing policy, Think-SFT runs past the cap on the same long problems the base does (24 of its 46 misses are cap hits), so by the theory its rescue of T1 cap hits falls well below its matched rate on finished-wrong problems: about 0.3 against 0.6, a difference near -0.3, far below the -0.05 the advocate gives RL. This rival puts the reward-free arm near RL's own matched excess, about -0.07.

r5-m10-rival.rival: The plain base's terse register is intrinsically weaker than the deliberative '\nOkay' register by about 15-20 points at any temperature, and the extra loss at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 is mostly a stopping-and-grading failure, not derailed reasoning: after writing its answer the terse register often fails to sample end-of-text and runs on into further 'Answer:' lines or invented follow-up problems, so the last-marker grader v3 scores a later, wrong answer over a first answer that was often right, while the deliberative register ends on one final answer.

rows.experiment: First-marker regrade of the plain base's wrong non-self-opened answers at T 1.0: among non-self-opened T3 rows graded wrong by grader v3 on the full text, the fraction whose first answer marker is right.
rows.theory_should_say: The theory says terse answers fail because tail tokens derail the solution after its opening, so the first stated answer is already wrong and a first-marker regrade recovers almost nothing (about 0.03, like the cued T1 rows' 0.0). In the rival, a sizable share of these failures are right answers overwritten by run-on text.

rows.experiment: Direction of first/last disagreement in the plain base's non-self-opened T 1.0 answers: among rows where the first-marker grade differs from the v3 last-marker grade, the share that are first-right and last-wrong.
rows.theory_should_say: The theory has the terse register neither revising nor running on: its errors come from corrupted reasoning, so first and last markers rarely disagree and, when they do, disagree in either direction about equally (about 0.45). In the rival, disagreements are mostly a right answer followed by a wrong run-on answer.

rows.experiment: Run-on share among the plain base's finished, wrong, non-self-opened T 1.0 answers: the fraction that keep going for more than 300 characters after their first answer marker and state another answer marker.
rows.theory_should_say: The theory has wrong terse answers going off course before or at their answer and then stopping, so few of them restate a new answer more than 300 characters later (about 0.15). In the rival, running on past the answer is the main way these rows end up wrong.

rows.experiment: Within the cued base's MATH-500 answers at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0: accuracy of answers containing 'Wait' or 'Hmm' minus accuracy of answers containing neither.
rows.theory_should_say: The theory makes self-checking the reason the deliberative register survives untruncated sampling, so cued answers that check themselves should be at least as accurate as those that do not (about +0.05). In the rival, checks only mark long, hard problems, and unchecked cued answers are short and nearly always right, so the difference is clearly negative.

rows.experiment: The same contrast on the harder clean 328: within cued base answers at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, accuracy of answers containing 'Wait' or 'Hmm' minus accuracy of answers containing neither.
rows.theory_should_say: Under the theory, self-checks are what lets the deliberative register survive full-temperature noise, so checked cued answers should be no worse than unchecked ones (about 0, maybe slightly positive). The rival expects a strongly negative gap: unchecked answers are the few short, easy ones, and the checked ones include all 77 cap hits.

rows.experiment: Gold-in-text excess at T 1.0 over T 0.6 for the plain base's finished, wrong, non-self-opened answers on problems with an integer gold of absolute value >= 10: the share whose text contains the gold number, T 1.0 minus T 0.6.
rows.theory_should_say: In the theory, wrong terse answers at T 1.0 are reasoning derailed by tail tokens, so they reach the gold no more often than the genuine mistakes at T 0.6 (about 0.0). In the rival, many T 1.0 failures wrote the right number and then lost it by running on, so the share is clearly higher at T 1.0.

r5-m03-rival.rival: The top-8 edit installs a weak dose of RL's policy on every sample, but on a fixed subset of prompts the plain prompt still keys the plain base's own short, committed answer, so top8 plain's quick wrong answers are a per-problem plain-prompt failure: they fall on the problems that the unedited plain base itself gets wrong, not on random samples drawn at a flat ~50 % error rate whatever the problem.

rows.experiment: Plain-base T 1.0 wrong rate on the problems where top8 plain gives a quick finished-wrong answer.
rows.theory_should_say: If the plain-register failure is a per-sample coin flip that ignores the problem, an independent plain-base sample on these mostly cued-easy problems is wrong at about its usual rate on such problems, about 0.45-0.5. The rival says the same prompts trip the plain base, which gives about 0.7.

rows.experiment: Difficulty-controlled contrast: plain-base T 1.0 wrong rate on top8's quick-wrong problems minus its wrong rate on top8-right problems that the cued base solves in at least 3 of 4 samples.
rows.theory_should_say: Under per-sample switching, which problems fail is unrelated to the plain base's own failures beyond difficulty. Q is only slightly harder than C for the cued base, so the theory implies a small gap of about 0.0-0.1, against the rival's 0.25.

rows.experiment: Plain-base T 0.6 wrong rate (a second, independent plain sample) on the problems where top8 plain gives a quick finished-wrong answer.
rows.theory_should_say: The plain base at T 0.6 is right on 319/500 overall and more often on cued-easy problems. If top8's quick failures are sample-level chance, this independent sample is wrong on about 0.3-0.35 of Q. The rival puts the failure in the prompt and expects about 0.55.

rows.experiment: Difficulty dependence of the plain register at T 1.0. Among plain-base T 1.0 answers that do not self-open, accuracy on problems the cued base solves in all 4 Day-1 #3 samples minus accuracy on problems it solves in at most 1 of 4.
rows.theory_should_say: The advocate's plain register is wrong about half the time whatever the difficulty, so its accuracy is the same on cued-easy and cued-hard problems, a difference near 0 (within about +-0.15). The rival puts plain-base failures on hard problems, so the gap is about 0.4.

rows.experiment: Difficulty dependence of the plain register at T 0.6. The same contrast on the plain base's T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 answers that do not self-open: accuracy on cued-4/4 problems minus accuracy on cued <= 1/4 problems.
rows.theory_should_say: With the plain register at a flat ~0.36 wrong rate whatever the difficulty, accuracy on cued-easy and cued-hard problems would match, a gap near 0. The rival expects a gap of about 0.55.

rows.experiment: Per-problem persistence of plain-base failures at fixed difficulty. On problems the cued base solves in all 4 samples, the plain-base T 1.0 wrong rate when the plain-base T 0.6 answer to the same problem is wrong, minus the T 1.0 wrong rate when that T 0.6 answer is right.
rows.theory_should_say: Under the advocate's account, plain-register errors are independent per-sample draws that ignore the problem, so on a fixed set of cued-easy problems a T 0.6 failure says nothing about the T 1.0 sample, giving a - b near 0 (about -0.1 to +0.1). The rival's per-problem failures give about 0.22.
